content: Cultural references to stuttering are frequently depicted in media, popular culture, and society. The unique characteristics of stuttering, including its distinct speech patterns and associated behaviors, have made it a subject of scientific inquiry, curiosity, discrimination, and ridicule. In literature, Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, was denied the opportunity to become a priest due to his stuttering. In response, he wrote a poem that humorously referenced stuttering, including lines like, Learn well your grammar / And never stammer. Carroll’s stuttering is subtly alluded to in Alice in Wonderland through the character of the Dodo bird, which Martin Gardner noted was drawn to resemble Carroll. Carroll himself often pronounced his last name as Do-Do-Dodgson. In film, stuttering has been explored in various ways. In A Fish Called Wanda (1988), Michael Palin’s character has a severe stutter and low self-esteem, embodying a stereotypical portrayal of stutterers as socially awkward and reclusive. The film’s other characters represent a spectrum of reactions to stuttering: one is sympathetic, another indifferent, and a third malicious. The film sparked controversy, with some stutterers criticizing its portrayal of Palin’s character as a victim of bullying, while others appreciated its depiction of the challenges faced by stutterers. Palin, whose father also stuttered, aimed to highlight the pain and difficulty of stuttering through his role. He later founded the Michael Palin Centre for Stammering Children in London. The 1983 film The Right Stuff depicted the real-life stuttering of Annie Glenn, the wife of astronaut John Glenn. Her stuttering caused her to avoid public speaking, but she later underwent intensive speech therapy and successfully managed her symptoms. A significant moment for her was delivering her first public speech about her experiences as a stutterer. In One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, the character Billy Bibbit struggles with a pronounced stutter that severely impacts his self-esteem, even leading to a suicide attempt after being mocked for stuttering during a marriage proposal. His stutter temporarily disappears after a sexual encounter but returns later in the story. In Rocket Science, the main character Hal Hefner deals with stuttering, while in M. Night Shyamalan’s Lady in the Water, Paul Giamatti’s character has a stutter that selectively disappears during interactions with another character. In Stephen King’s IT, the character Bill Denbrough stutters more intensely when scared or nervous, but he overcomes his stutter temporarily before it resurfaces. On television, the animated character Porky Pig from Looney Tunes is one of the most famous fictional stutterers. Originally voiced by an actual stutterer, the role was later taken over by Mel Blanc, who mimicked the stutter. In 1991, the National Stuttering Project protested Warner Bros., urging them to use Porky Pig as an advocate for children with stuttering rather than as a source of ridicule. Warner Bros. eventually donated to the Stuttering Foundation of America and released anti-bullying public service announcements. An episode of MASH featured a stuttering soldier who believed he was unintelligent due to his speech impediment. Major Winchester, a typically pompous character, proved the soldier’s intelligence and gifted him a treasured copy of Moby-Dick. At the end of the episode, it is revealed that Winchester’s sister also has a pronounced stutter. In Open All Hours, Ronnie Barker’s character has a stutter that sometimes causes trouble, and his nephew mocks him for it. Actor Nicholas Brendon, who played Xander Harris on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, overcame his stuttering and became a spokesperson for the Stuttering Foundation of America. On South Park, the character Jimmy Vulmer has a severe stutter that is often used for comedic effect. In music, stuttering has been used as a stylistic device. The 1918 song K-K-K-Katy became a wartime hit, using stuttered lyrics to portray a bashful suitor. Buddy Holly frequently employed stuttering and other vocal tics in his songs. The Who’s 1965 song My Generation famously features stuttering in its lyrics, as does Bachman-Turner Overdrive’s 1974 hit You Ain’t Seen Nothing Yet, which was initially intended as a joke about Randy Bachman’s stuttering brother. By the 1980s, producers began creating stuttering effects synthetically through tape editing and sampling, as seen in Paul Hardcastle’s 1985 song 19. However, the use of stuttering in music declined in the 1990s. In 1995, Scatman John turned his stuttering into an asset with his hit song Scatman, which combined scat singing with inspirational lyrics aimed at stutterers. Other examples include Joe’s 2001 song Stutter, Placebo’s use of a stammering voice in their 1996 song Swallow, and Teddy Geiger’s For You I Will (Confidence), which references stuttering in its lyrics. Bloc Party’s lead singer Kele Okereke has a pronounced stutter when speaking but not when singing. Finally, in radio, John Melendez, known as Stuttering John, became a star on Howard Stern’s show despite his mild stutter. Stern also featured other guests with speech impediments, often using their conditions for comedic purposes while maintaining a sense of affection and inclusion for them among his audience.
